summary: Teach two ideas in order for ages 7–9: (1) foods are sorted into the food groups of an appropriate local healthy-eating guide (the UK Eatwell Guide's five groups; in Australia, the five food groups of the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating), while nutrients are taught separately — what foods supply and the job each does (carbohydrates for energy; proteins for growth and repair; fats for energy, warmth and storage; vitamins, minerals and fibre, with water, for keeping the body working and protected), recognising that most foods supply several nutrients; and (2) a balanced diet means a variety of foods from each food group in the RIGHT AMOUNTS shown by the guide, not just having a bit of everything. The nutrient→job layer is easier; the proportion/balance idea is the harder, more valuable one and explains why 'eat lots of everything' and 'fat is bad' are wrong. Proportions belong to food groups, never to equal shares of nutrients (the UK Eatwell Guide, which replaced the earlier Eatwell plate in 2016: fruit/veg and starchy carbs biggest, protein and dairy smaller, oils/spreads tiny, sugary/fatty treats outside and occasional). Build balanced plates by hand rather than reciting rules, surface that mixed dishes (pizza, sandwiches) combine several food groups, and frame balance over a day or week rather than per-meal perfection. Avoid calorie counting; keep to food groups, nutrient jobs and rough proportions.
misconceptions: Calling nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins) 'food groups', or imagining a balanced plate as equal shares of seven nutrients — food groups are groups of foods in a healthy-eating guide, and proportions follow those groups.
'Fat (or carbs, or sugar) is bad and should be avoided' — missing that fats/carbs are needed for energy; it's balance and amount that matter.
'A balanced diet means eating a bit of everything equally' — missing that the PROPORTIONS differ (more fruit/veg and starchy food, less oil).
'Each food supplies just one nutrient' or 'a mixed dish fits one food group' — pizza and sandwiches combine several food groups, and foods such as milk supply several nutrients.
'Vitamins/minerals give you energy' — they protect and help the body work; energy comes mainly from carbohydrates and fats.
'Healthy food = salad only / treats are forbidden' — rather than occasional treats fitting within an overall balance.
'You must eat perfectly at every meal' — missing that balance is judged over a day or week.
'Protein is only meat' — missing beans, pulses, eggs, dairy and fish as protein sources.

activities.title: Build a balanced plate
steps: Collect real or pictured everyday foods the child actually eats, then sort each into the food groups of a local healthy-eating guide (Eatwell: fruit and vegetables; starchy carbohydrates; proteins; dairy and alternatives; oils and spreads, with treats outside the main groups — or the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating's five food groups).

Arrange foods onto a plate divided into the guide's food-group proportions (with Eatwell, fruit/veg and starchy foods fill the largest areas, protein and dairy smaller areas, oils/spreads a tiny area, and sugary/fatty treats sit off to the side as occasional).
Deliberately try an unbalanced plate — a mountain of chips only, or nothing but fruit — and describe which food groups are missing and which nutrient jobs may not be covered.

As each food is placed, say its food group and one main nutrient it supplies and what that nutrient does (e.g. bread: starchy food, supplies carbohydrate for energy; chicken: protein food, supplies protein for growth and repair), noting that most foods supply several nutrients.
Look across a whole day or week and check whether one wobbly meal is evened out by the others.
activities.insight: Balance is not 'a bit of everything equally' — it is the right amounts of each food group, with (in the Eatwell Guide) fruit/veg and starchy foods making up most of the plate and treats only occasional; and balance is judged over a day or week, not at every single meal.

activities.title: Match each nutrient to its job
steps: Reveal, one nutrient at a time, what each nutrient does for the body and list foods that supply it: carbohydrates = energy; protein = growth and repair; fats = energy, warmth and storage; vitamins and minerals = protection and keeping the body working; fibre = digestion; water = hydration.
For each nutrient, predict and then check what might happen if you had too much or too little of it.

Name at least five nutrients with a food that supplies each, say which food group each food belongs to, notice foods (such as milk) that supply several nutrients, and explain the job of carbohydrates, proteins and fats in your own words.
activities.insight: Each nutrient does a distinct job; vitamins and minerals protect and help the body work but do NOT supply energy — energy comes mainly from carbohydrates and fats.

activities.title: Sort mixed foods
steps: Classify everyday foods into the guide's food-group bins, including a dedicated 'mixed foods' bin.
Break down mixed dishes — a pizza, a sandwich — into the food groups their ingredients come from, naming each part, and list the several nutrients a single food such as a glass of milk supplies.
Discuss why a mixed dish draws on several food groups, and why even a single food supplies several nutrients.
activities.insight: Mixed dishes combine foods from several food groups, and most foods supply several nutrients, so neither classification is one-to-one.

activities.title: Myth-busting: is this food bad for me?
steps: Pose 'is X bad for me?' questions and answer using nutrient jobs and overall balance rather than a 'good food / bad food' verdict.

Consider Sam's claim that fat is always bad and should be avoided completely — explain why the body still needs some fat (for energy, warmth and storage) and that it is the amount and balance that matter, not banning a whole nutrient.

Work through the swimmer example: Sam says he'll eat lots of oranges and take vitamin tablets because 'vitamins give you energy and make you strong' — decide whether to agree and explain what he should eat for energy (carbohydrates: bread, pasta, rice) and for building muscle (protein: chicken, fish, eggs, beans), and why each helps.
Reason about what might go wrong on race day if someone ate only protein and no carbohydrates, and why we still need vitamins regularly in our food even though they give no energy.
activities.insight: No single food or nutrient is simply 'bad' or 'banned' — even fats are needed for energy, warmth and storage; it is the overall balance and amount across a day or week that matters, and each nutrient must be matched to the job it actually does.

checkQuestion: Sam is training for a swimming race and wants stronger muscles. He says 'I'll eat lots of oranges and take vitamin tablets, because vitamins give you energy and make you strong.' Do you agree with Sam's plan? What SHOULD he eat for energy and for building muscle — and why does each food help with its job?
checkAnswer: Disagree with Sam. Vitamins don't give energy or directly build muscle — they help the body work properly and protect it from illness. For energy he needs carbohydrates (bread, pasta, rice); for building and repairing muscle he needs protein (chicken, fish, eggs, beans). What matters is the JOB each nutrient does, not whether a food merely seems 'healthy'.
